extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, IP office officials, patent and trademark practitioners, and negotiators working on IP law reform in the EU and GCC countries
extracted.subtask_short: GCC GI and patent legal standards
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the legal criteria, definitions, scope, exclusions, and procedural rules governing geographical indications (GIs), trademarks and patents across GCC countries, with country-specific notes and recommendations for harmonization with international instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt EU Directive 2015/2436 as model for trademark reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation that GCC countries can benefit from the EU Directive 2015/2436 on approximation of trademark laws as a model to improve their existing systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Directive as a model to modernize national regimes; harmonization can simplify cross-border trademark protection and procedural standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to the Singapore Treaty on the Law of Trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation that GCC countries adhere to the Singapore Treaty which builds on the Trademark Law Treaty but has a wider scope addressing recent developments in communication technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adherence will modernize systems and harmonize procedures with signatory countries; it would help resolve procedural difficulties such as adoption of the Nice Classification, elimination of single-class-per-application rules, and removal of notarization/legalization requirements for documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indication (GI) definition (TRIPS)
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs defined as 'indications which identify a good as originating in the territory of a Member, or a region or locality in that territory, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of the good is essentially attributable to its geographical origin' (Article 22 TRIPS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This TRIPS definition is reflected in the sui generis laws of Bahrain, Qatar and Oman; countries applying unified trademark law may not define GIs explicitly, which affects protection scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of protection for GIs
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of GI protection includes agricultural and non-agricultural products including handicrafts (varies by country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country examples: Bahrain, Qatar, Oman cover agricultural and industrial products/handicrafts; several countries protect 'all goods classes available for trademarks'. Check national lists/tables for exact coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: International instruments relevant to GI protection
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs protection is linked to international agreements: Paris Convention, Madrid Agreement (repression of false indications), Lisbon Agreement (appellations of origin), and TRIPS; GCC countries are members of Paris Convention and TRIPS, Oman is in final phase of adhering to Geneva Act of Lisbon Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adherence to additional treaties (e.g., Geneva Act of Lisbon, Madrid Agreement) is recommended to strengthen cross-border enforcement and recognition of GIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: GIs and wines & spirits—public order exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Although TRIPS provides additional protection for wines and spirits, GCC countries applying Islamic Sharia that forbids alcoholic beverages are unlikely to recognize or register foreign GIs for wines and spirits on grounds that such goods violate public order or morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect non-recognition of wine and spirits GIs (and related trademarks) in many GCC jurisdictions; this limits the effect of TRIPS' enhanced protection for those products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for denying GI protection / registrability
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs are not protected or registrable if they: do not comply with the law's GI definition; are contrary to public order or morality; are not or cease to be protected in their country of origin; have fallen into disuse in the country of origin; are identical with or customary common names; are confusingly similar to an existing or pending trademark registered in good faith; or where registration as a trademark is impermissible under trademark law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country-specific formulations: Bahrain, Oman and Qatar state variants of these exclusions (see tables). National practice may also allow exceptions for prior good-faith use, personal names used without misleading the public, and cases where the GI is generic in local language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural treatment of GIs (registration, examination, opposition, remedies)
rubrics_metrics.description: In several GCC countries GIs applications follow trademark procedures (filing, examination, acceptance/rejection, opposition, cancellation/strike-off, transfer, licensing, seizure, compensation). Courts may grant injunctions, award damages, and impose criminal penalties for GI infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qatar: GIs follow trademark rules and can be protected even if unregistered; Oman: provides an operational GI registration system; Bahrain & Qatar may still be pending implementing regulations. Ensure registries (Geographical Indications Register) and by-laws are established for effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of protection for GIs
rubrics_metrics.description: Term of protection varies: Oman indicates the term of protection for GIs is unlimited; Qatar provides protection for ten years renewable indefinitely for terms of ten years each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check national law for renewal mechanics and whether unregistered GIs enjoy any protection under unfair competition rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for EU assistance on GIs
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended EU cooperation actions: conduct surveys on GI awareness, help sectors understand pros/cons, share EU best practices, identify GI products with reputation and export potential, suggest protection schemes, assist in law/regulation drafting and producer organization, share supply chain and product specification methods, provide capacity building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial approach: pilot projects per country; avoid focusing on wine/spirits initially; encourage adherence to Madrid Agreement and Geneva Act of the Lisbon Treaty after operational GI registries are in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents shall be granted for inventions in all fields of technology provided they are new, involve an inventive step, and are susceptible of industrial application (in line with TRIPS and EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This triad (novelty, inventive step/non-obviousness, industrial applicability/utility) is applied across GCC patent laws, with national definitions and interpretations. Use EPC/ TRIPS standards as benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omani definitions and extended patentable subject-matter (new uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omani law provides clear definitions of 'novelty', 'inventive step' and 'industrial applicability' and extends patent protection to 'any new uses for, or new methods of using, a known product, including new uses and new methods for the treatment of particular medical conditions'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extension goes beyond TRIPS and EPC and may affect generics; report recommends Oman revisits its law (e.g., refer to EPC Articles 53–54) or use TRIPS flexibilities to limit scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of computer-implemented inventions (Oman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omani law provides for patentability of computer-implemented inventions including: (a) industrial processes that in whole or in part consist of steps performed by a computer and directed by a computer program; (b) product inventions consisting of elements of a computer-implemented invention (i) machine-readable computer program code stored on a tangible medium; (ii) a general purpose computer whose novelty arises primarily from its combination with a specific computer program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a national substantive allowance; note that computer-implemented inventions remain unsettled in other jurisdictions (EU attempted harmonization and failed in 2005). Consult national practice for examination standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art and 'novelty' considerations (Oman and general)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is new if not anticipated by prior art. Prior art consists of everything disclosed to the public anywhere by publication in tangible form, oral disclosure, use, or any other way prior to filing or priority date. Certain disclosures within twelve months preceding filing by reason of acts committed by applicant or predecessor or due to abuse by a third party may not be taken into consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omani law specifies these prior art / grace-like rules; national statutes differ on grace periods and exceptions—examine national text for precise treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step / non-obviousness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention involves an inventive step if it would not have been obvious to a person skilled in the art at the filing date or priority date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard used across GCC laws; apply the 'person skilled in the art' test when assessing inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability / utility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is industrially applicable if it can be made or used in any kind of industry or if it has specific, substantial and credible utility, including in economic, agricultural, handicrafts, fisheries and services fields (broad wording in some GCC laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National laws may adopt broad or narrow notions of 'industrial applicability'; check particular country wording (Oman, UAE, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention / single-invention requirement (UAE)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must be restricted to one invention or a group of interrelated inventions; the UAE law limits an application to one invention or an interrelated group yielding an innovative concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may require restriction or division if unity is not met; evidence post-issuance that interrelationship was absent does not necessarily negate the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability (general GCC list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common exclusions across GCC laws include: discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, computer programs (varied treatment), schemes/rules/methods for doing business, purely mental acts, games, plant varieties, animal species, biological processes for producing plants/animals (with exceptions for microbiological processes and products), methods of surgical/therapeutic/diagnostic treatment of humans/animals (exceptions for products used in such methods), natural substances, and known substances for which a new use has been discovered (country-specific).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each GCC country frames exclusions slightly differently (see Table 15). Oman, for example, explicitly excludes natural substances and known substances with new uses but protects isolation processes and uses when those constitute inventions. Check each national exclusion list carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions based on Sharia / public order and morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some GCC laws and the GCC Patent Regulation add exclusions for inventions that may conflict with the principles of Islamic Sharia or that are contrary to public order or morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saudi Arabia and GCC-level regulation explicitly include Sharia-based exclusions; this can impact the patentability of methods, products or uses deemed impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: National security special procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE apply special procedures (to be detailed in implementing regulations) concerning inventions that affect national security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent offices may implement confidentiality measures, special examination or restrictions for security-sensitive inventions under national implementing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for isolation processes and uses of natural substances (Oman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omani law excludes natural substances from patentability but does not apply that exclusion to processes of isolating those natural substances from their original environment; the law also does not exclude the use itself where it constitutes an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This carve-out means isolating processes and inventive uses of known natural substances can be protected—evaluate claims for process vs product scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and remedies for GI infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts can grant injunctions to prevent unlawful use of GIs, award damages, and grant appropriate remedies; infringements of registered GIs are punishable offences (e.g., forging or imitating GIs, unlawfully using or selling goods bearing forged or imitated GIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qatar explicitly provides protection even for unregistered GIs; criminal and civil remedies may apply. Effective enforcement depends on the existence of operational registries and implementing regulations.
